overview: This file assembles U.S. diplomatic and consular records concerning the censorship, opening, damage, and detention of foreign mail by Japanese military, postal, or other authorities, principally during 1938–1939. It includes cross-reference sheets for reports from Shanghai, China, Tianjin, Qingdao, and Batavia; a detailed Tianjin despatch with postal-service replies concerning damaged correspondence and censored copies of Reader’s Digest; and an embassy despatch documenting an Iranian protest over mail opened in Japan. The final cross-reference concerns mail from China reportedly detained at Shanghai because American President Lines vessels were allegedly barred from carrying it across the Pacific. Several documents expose the tension between officials’ private acknowledgment of Japanese censorship and their unwillingness or inability to admit it formally.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on censorship of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report that official censors opened and read mail sent to or from foreigners in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference directs the reader to file 125.9256/47 and report no. 1177 from Gauss at Shanghai. It states that all personal and official mail involving foreigners in Taiwan, particularly foreign officials, was opened and carefully read by official censors.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference on censorship of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan
subfiles.about: A duplicate sheet records systematic examination of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: This sheet repeats the reference to file 125.9256/47 and report no. 1177 concerning censorship in Taiwan. Its OCR date reads 1933, but the otherwise identical sheet and surrounding file context indicate 1938.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on examination of official American mail at Harbin
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report concerning the examination of official American mail at Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart transmitted to the embassy a report from the American Consulate General at Tianjin concerning official American mail at Harbin. The original material is cross-referenced to file 125.4616/70 as report no. 1546.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Caldwell’s initial report on censorship at Tianjin
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes an initial report on censored American mail and a promise of inquiry by the Japanese Consul General.
subfiles.summary: Caldwell reported censorship of American mail at Tianjin. Japanese Consul General Horiuchi reportedly promised to investigate the matter; the report is cross-referenced as despatch no. 612 in file 125.9536/46.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Caldwell’s supplementary report on censorship at Tianjin
subfiles.about: The sheet records the absence of official information about tampered mail and a Japanese assurance that complaints would not recur.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference summarizes Caldwell’s supplementary report on American mail at Tianjin. Although no information about the tampering could officially be obtained, Consul Tanaka assured Caldwell that there would be no further cause for complaint. The OCR date of 1958 is an evident error for 1938.

subfiles.title: Caldwell despatch on Japanese military censorship of American mail
subfiles.from: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Beijing
subfiles.about: Caldwell reports privately acknowledged Japanese military interference with American consular mail and encloses three postal replies and a damaged envelope.
subfiles.summary: Caldwell supplements his April 7 despatch with three communications from the acting Director of Posts for Hebei, all claiming that investigations had failed to establish where the mail was tampered with. Caldwell states that the postal director knew Japanese military censors were responsible but was in too precarious a position to say so officially. The Japanese Consul General did not deny military responsibility and reported having raised the matter at Japanese military headquarters in Beijing, where assurances against recurrence were given.

subfiles.title: Caretti letter acknowledging two American postal complaints
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, U.S. Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti acknowledges complaints about irregularities affecting mail addressed to American consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: Caretti reports that Caldwell’s March 28 complaint had been referred to the Peiping Road Post Office after the initial inquiry produced no result. He also states that a second complaint made that day was under investigation and promises to communicate the results.

subfiles.title: Caretti reply concerning the opened Chang Fong Mee envelope
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti reports that postal inquiries could not establish responsibility for apparent tampering with an embassy letter.
subfiles.summary: The letter concerns an ordinary letter from the American Embassy at Beijing to Mrs. Chang Fong Mee, care of the Tianjin consulate, whose envelope appeared to have been opened and resealed. Caretti says inquiries at both Tianjin and Beijing yielded no evidence that the irregularity occurred while the letter was in postal custody. He suggests that machinery or friction in a mailbag might explain the damaged seal and returns the envelope.

subfiles.title: Caretti reply concerning censored copies of Reader’s Digest
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti responds to a protest that pages had been removed from magazines addressed to American consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: Caldwell had protested that pages were torn from the April 1938 copies of Reader’s Digest sent to him and his staff, although the wrappers bore no censor’s stamp. Caretti reports that an investigation failed to determine where this happened. He acknowledges that the magazines were held until released by censors but notes that, as unregistered matter, they generated no tracking record.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Grew’s Iranian protest despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: An internal review note dismisses the need for action on the Iranian protest over opened diplomatic mail in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Tokyo despatch no. 3156 concerning an Iranian protest against Japanese postal authorities. It characterizes the protest’s tone and lack of supporting evidence as indicative of Iranian international methods and states that the despatch need not be read. No action was recommended.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch transmitting the Iranian protest
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits an Iranian diplomatic protest over an opened letter and compares it with American experience involving mail to Taipei.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses the diplomatic corps dean’s circular and the Iranian Chargé d’Affaires’ protest over mail allegedly opened by Japanese postal authorities. He criticizes the protest as violent and unsupported by evidence that Japanese officials were responsible or that the event formed part of a pattern. He nevertheless notes that the embassy possessed a cover addressed to the American Consul at Taihoku bearing five wax seals from American offices, which it informally showed to a Japanese Foreign Office official while observing that confidential matter was never sent there by ordinary mail.

subfiles.title: Bassompierre circular on the Iranian mail complaint
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.to: Members of the Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The dean circulates Sheybany’s protest while declining for the moment to intervene collectively.
subfiles.summary: At Sheybany’s request, Bassompierre sends his diplomatic colleagues a copy of the Iranian protest addressed to Foreign Minister Ugaki. He says there is presently no reason for the diplomatic corps to intervene. He would reconsider if further violations suggested a systematic practice rather than an isolated or accidental incident.

subfiles.title: Sheybany protest over opened Iranian diplomatic mail
subfiles.to: General Kazushige Ugaki, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Sheybany formally protests two incidents involving opened mail addressed to the Iranian Legation and threatens reciprocal action.
subfiles.summary: Sheybany recalls an earlier parcel from Iran that arrived open through the Azabu post office despite subsequent assurances from Hirota and postal officials. He now refuses a registered letter from Williamstown, Australia, because it was offered to the Iranian Legation in a completely open condition. Invoking private rights, international law, and diplomatic immunity, he demands dismissal of the responsible official, delivery of the letter with an apology, and guarantees against repetition; otherwise Iran might open mail addressed to the Japanese Legation in Tehran.

subfiles.title: English translation of Bassompierre’s circular note
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.to: Members of the Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The enclosure translates the dean’s French circular concerning the Iranian request for collective diplomatic action.
subfiles.summary: The translation records Bassompierre’s circulation of Sheybany’s July 19 letter to Foreign Minister Ugaki. Bassompierre provisionally declines to make representations for the diplomatic corps as a whole. He leaves open the possibility of action if additional reports demonstrate systematic violations of diplomatic correspondence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on censorship of the American Consulate’s mail at Qingdao
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report and protest concerning Japanese detention of an American consular letter at Qingdao.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin submitted a report on Japanese censorship of the American Consulate’s mail. He also addressed a protest to the Japanese Consul General at Qingdao concerning the detention of a consular letter. The original is cross-referenced as report no. 348 in file 125.9536/50.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese censorship of mail at Batavia
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on Japanese mail censorship accompanied by an envelope that had been opened.
subfiles.summary: Dickover submitted a report concerning censorship of mail by Japanese authorities. An opened envelope accompanied the report as physical evidence. The original document is cross-referenced to file 135.1776/111 as report no. 146.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on mail from China detained at Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an inquiry into reports that U.S.-bound mail was being held at Shanghai because American President Lines vessels could not carry it across the Pacific.
subfiles.summary: The underlying telegram quoted a November 7 New York Herald Tribune despatch claiming that mail from China for the United States was detained at Shanghai because the U.S. Maritime Commission had prohibited its transportation on American President Lines vessels. The Maritime Commission told the Department that it had issued no such order. A report on the situation was therefore requested from Shanghai.

interest: The file is especially useful for comparing private diplomatic knowledge with official postal denials: Caldwell states that both Chinese postal and Japanese consular officials effectively knew Japanese military censors were responsible, although the postal director dared not admit it. The surviving postal replies illustrate the bureaucratic explanations—machinery, mailbag friction, and lack of registration records—used to avoid assigning responsibility. The Iranian correspondence adds a revealing contrast between a forceful appeal to international law and the skeptical, even dismissive assessment made by American diplomats, while Grew’s reference to American mail for Taihoku shows that the problem extended beyond China. Taken together, the records illuminate censorship practices, diplomatic privilege, informal protest, and the evidentiary difficulties surrounding interference with international mail in Japan’s imperial sphere.
